item.title: Prognostic Value of Thromboelastography Parameters for Early Trauma-Induced Coagulopathy in Severely Injured Patients: A Retrospective Cohort Study
item.category: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine
item.description:
Background and importance: Early trauma-induced coagulopathy (eTIC) is a major contributor to hemorrhage-related mortality after severe trauma. Viscoelastic testing using thromboelastography (TEG) has been increasingly implemented in trauma resuscitation; however, its prognostic value compared with conventional coagulation testing remains uncertain.

Objectives: We evaluated the ability of TEG parameters to detect eTIC, hypofibrinogenemia, and hyperfibrinolysis in severely injured trauma patients. In addition, we assessed their prognostic performance for transfusion requirements and mortality compared with conventional laboratory parameters.

Design: Retrospective single-center cohort study.

Settings and participants: Severely injured adult trauma patients admitted to the resuscitation room of a Level I trauma center, between January 2019 and October 2024 were screened.

Outcome measures and analysis: Primary outcomes were detection of eTIC (INR > 1.2), severe coagulopathy (INR > 1.5), hypofibrinogenemia (< 200 mg/dL), and thrombocytopenia (< 100,000/μL). Secondary outcomes included the ability of coagulation parameters to predict the need for transfusion of ≥ 5 units of packed red blood cells within the first 24 h after admission and in-hospital mortality.

Results: A total of 262 patients were included; median ISS was 29 (IQR 23-41), and in-hospital mortality was 22.8%. eTIC was present in 31.5% of patients. TEG parameters showed moderate discriminatory performance for coagulopathy detection. For eTIC, maximum amplitude achieved an AUC of 0.73, while R-time achieved an AUC of 0.65. Predictive performance improved for severe coagulopathy, with R-time reaching an AUC of 0.81. Hyperfibrinolysis (LY30 > 7%) was uncommon (6.9%). Conventional laboratory parameters, particularly INR, consistently outperformed TEG-derived parameters for prediction of transfusion requirements (AUC 0.85) and mortality (AUC 0.79).

Conclusion: In severely injured trauma patients, conventional coagulation testing, particularly INR, demonstrated superior prognostic performance compared with individual TEG parameters. Viscoelastic testing may provide complementary information but did not replace standard laboratory testing for prediction of transfusion needs or mortality in this cohort.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT07186712.

Honnef G, Zoidl P, Hallmann B, Missmann M, Eichinger M, Niederer M
Journal Article, Observational Study

item.title: Reliability and Validity of the Australian Mental Health Triage Scale in Children's Hospitals
item.category: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine
item.description:
Objective: To evaluate interrater reliability and validity of the Australian Mental Health Triage Scale (AMHTS) for children presenting to the emergency department (ED) with behavioral health symptoms.

Methods: We conducted a prospective observational study of ED visits by children aged 3-17 with a primary behavioral health symptom at two US children's hospitals. Nurses assigned Emergency Severity Index (ESI) and AMHTS Scores. Interrater reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) on visits with two independently assigned AMHTS Scores. To evaluate validity, quasi-Poisson regression examined the association of AMHTS Scores and ED resource utilization, adjusted for sociodemographic and clinical factors. Resource use was categorized using the standard ESI definition and an expanded definition incorporating behavioral health-specific resources.

Results: We included 454 visits (45.4% aged 10-14, 56.2% female) with at least one AMHTS Score, of which 94.1% were ESI 2 and 26.9% were AMHTS 2. Among 221 visits with two AMHTS Scores, ICC was 0.48 (95% CI 0.37, 0.58). Higher-acuity AMHTS Scores were associated with greater resource utilization. Standard resource use was higher for AMHTS Score 1 (Incidence Rate Ratio [IRR] 1.82, 95% CI 1.12, 2.96) and Score 2 (IRR 1.64, 95% CI 1.15, 2.40) versus AMHTS Score 5. When applying the expanded definition, resource use was higher for AMHTS Score 1-4 versus 5.

Conclusion: Interrater reliability of AMHTS was fair, and higher-acuity scores were associated with greater ED resource utilization. AMHTS Scores were more widely distributed than ESI Scores, suggesting a more responsive approach to pediatric behavioral health triage.

Foster AA, Grupp-Phelan J, Crone R, Brown M, Denicolo K, Farley K
